questions.q: What happened to Nokia when it grew conservative about new ideas?
a: Sales and profits fell as it lost its innovative edge
It was acquired by a larger rival almost overnight
It shifted successfully from phones into software
It kept leading the smartphone market for years
questions.why: The first lesson says Nokia stopped innovating as much and then saw its sales and profits decline.

questions.q: Why is it a mistake to value only the innovators in a company?
a: The people running today's business are equally important
Innovators rarely produce ideas that make money
Execution work can always be outsourced cheaply
Innovators need no resources to do their work
questions.why: The second lesson calls the executors the breadwinners of today and says both groups are equally important.

questions.q: What happened when Shen Kuo described planets orbiting the sun?
a: Nobody listened or funded him and the idea faded
He was celebrated throughout China for the discovery
He published it and transformed Chinese astronomy
He abandoned astronomy to pursue a political career
questions.why: The third lesson says no one wanted to hear or fund Shen Kuo, and the same idea was rediscovered half a century later.

questions.q: How does the book describe the origin of loonshot ideas?
a: They often begin as crazy ideas given room to flourish
They come from lone geniuses who need no help
They require huge budgets from the very first day
They emerge mainly during national emergencies
questions.why: The overview says great ideas appear in unexpected moments and need space and support to become real products.

questions.q: What mistake did the US make with radar before Pearl Harbor?
a: It knew about the innovation but did not pursue it
It shared the technology openly with its enemies
It relied on radar and ignored its navy
It funded radar but trained no operators
questions.why: The first lesson says America knew about Leo Young's radar but did not think it necessary at the time.
